questions.question: What are Optional and Union types in Python, and when do you use them?
questions.title: Optional and Union Types in Python
questions.direct_answer: A union says that a value may have one of several stated types, such as `int | str`. An optional type is the specific union `T | None`, meaning the value may be absent; `Optional[T]` is an equivalent older spelling, not a synonym for a parameter with a default.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can model multiple valid runtime shapes and handle each branch safely.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using `Optional` because an argument can be omitted even though `None` is not an accepted value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain narrowing and state that `X | Y` syntax requires Python 3.10 or newer.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: `int | str` means a value may be either an integer or a string.
`User | None` means a user may be present or absent.
`Optional[User]` and `User | None` express the same type relationship.
Check or narrow a union before using operations that belong to only one member.
The `|` type syntax starts in Python 3.10; older code uses `Union` and `Optional`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A union represents a value with more than one valid type. `int | str` tells a checker that either shape is expected, so code must use only shared operations or first discover which member it received.

An optional type is a union with `None`. `User | None` means a real `User` may be unavailable, and `Optional[User]` means exactly the same thing. It does not simply mean that a caller may omit the argument.

For example, a lookup can return `User | None`. The caller checks `if user is None` for the missing case; after that branch, the checker narrows the remaining path to `User`, so accessing `user.name` is safe.

I use a union when the alternatives are genuine parts of the API and each can be handled clearly. If many unrelated types accumulate, a common protocol, a tagged data model, or separate functions often communicates the design better.

`X | Y` and `X | None` require Python 3.10 or newer. On older supported versions, I write `Union[X, Y]` and `Optional[X]`. These annotations still do not validate incoming values at runtime.

sections.title: A union is a set of allowed possibilities
sections.content:
Before narrowing, a checker must assume that any member of the union could be present. It therefore permits only operations that are safe for every remaining member. A branch such as `isinstance(value, int)` splits that set: inside the branch the value is an integer, while the other path retains the alternatives that did not match.

`None` represents absence, not a failed conversion and not an empty value such as `0` or `""`. Including it makes absence part of the function's public contract, so callers are responsible for handling that state. If absence should be exceptional, raising a domain-specific exception may describe the API more honestly.

Unions are strongest when the alternatives have a clear reason. A parser accepting a numeric ID or its text form is understandable; a return type that mixes unrelated success values and error strings is harder to use than a dedicated result model or exception.

sections.title: Narrow the set before using a member
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  U[value: int or str or None] --> N{value is None?}
  N -->|Yes| M[Handle absence]
  N -->|No| I{value is int?}
  I -->|Yes| A[Integer operations]
  I -->|No| S[String operations]
```

sections.title: Handle every member of a union

questions.question: What is the difference between an optional argument and a value that can be None?
questions.title: Optional Arguments vs Optional Values
questions.direct_answer: An optional argument is one the caller may omit because the signature provides a default. A value that can be `None` needs a type such as `str | None`. These ideas are independent: `limit: int = 10` is omittable but never promises `None`, while `name: str | None` may be required yet accept `None`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you distinguish Python's argument-binding rules from a union that includes the None value.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding `Optional` to every parameter with a default or forgetting it when `None` is an actual accepted value.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show all four combinations: required or omittable, independently from accepting or rejecting None.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: A default makes an argument omittable at the call site.
`T | None` makes `None` a valid value for the parameter.
`count: int = 0` is omittable but does not accept `None` in its type contract.
`value: str | None` can be required while still accepting `None`.
Use `Optional[T]` only as the older equivalent spelling of `T | None`.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An optional argument and an optional value describe different parts of a function. An argument is optional when a caller can leave it out because the signature supplies a default. A value is optional in the typing sense when `None` is one of its valid values.

For example, `def page(limit: int = 20)` lets the caller omit `limit`, but passing `None` disagrees with the `int` contract. The default is an integer and no branch for `None` is promised.

By contrast, `def display_name(name: str | None)` requires the caller to supply an argument, but that argument may explicitly be `None`. The function must handle both a string and absence.

Both ideas can also appear together: `name: str | None = None` is omittable and accepts `None`. The modern union syntax is available from Python 3.10; `Optional[str] = None` is the equivalent form used for older versions.

I make this distinction because an unnecessary `None` widens every caller's work, while a missing `None` hides a real state. The annotation should match values the implementation truly supports, and the default should match the calling convenience the API intends.

sections.title: Two independent decisions in one parameter
sections.content:
Python's argument binder decides whether a call is complete. If a parameter has no default and the caller omits it, Python raises `TypeError`. That rule does not inspect type annotations. A default fills the missing argument before the function body starts.

The type contract answers a separate question: after binding, which values may the parameter hold? Including `None` requires the body to narrow or otherwise handle absence. Excluding it tells checked callers not to pass `None`, although ordinary Python still does not enforce that hint.

Keeping the two axes separate produces more precise APIs. A default of `None` is useful as a sentinel when no ordinary value can mean “not supplied,” but sometimes a private sentinel object is necessary when `None` itself is meaningful and must be distinguished from omission.

sections.title: Omission and None are separate axes
sections.content:
| Signature fragment | Caller may omit? | Caller may pass `None`? |
|---|---:|---:|
| `value: str` | No | No |
| `value: str = "default"` | Yes | No |
| `value: str | None` | No | Yes |
| `value: str | None = None` | Yes | Yes |

sections.title: See all four parameter contracts

questions.question: How do you safely narrow an Optional or Union value in Python?
questions.title: Narrowing Optional and Union Values
questions.direct_answer: Use a runtime condition that proves the current case, such as `value is None`, `isinstance(value, str)`, or a discriminating field. A static checker follows the branches and narrows the remaining possibilities, allowing member-specific operations only after the relevant type is established.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you handle every valid member rather than silencing a checker with a cast or ignore comment.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling a method immediately on `T | None` or using `cast` as if it performed a runtime check.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use an early return to remove the exceptional case and explain exhaustive handling of the remaining union members.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Use `is None` to handle the absent member of an optional type.
Use `isinstance` to distinguish ordinary runtime classes in a union.
After a proven branch, a checker narrows the value to the matching member.
An early return often leaves the main path with one simple type.
`cast()` changes the checker's belief but performs no runtime check.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Narrowing means proving which member of a union is present before using member-specific behaviour. For an optional value, I usually check `if value is None` and handle or return from that case first. The remaining path is then known to contain the non-None type.

For a union of runtime classes, `isinstance` is the normal tool. For example, if an identifier is `int | str`, the integer branch can do arithmetic and the string branch can call `strip()` after the checker has followed the condition.

I prefer checks that reflect the real data model. A tagged record may narrow through a literal `kind` field, while a class hierarchy may narrow through `isinstance`. Truthiness alone is often wrong because `0`, `""`, and empty collections are valid values distinct from `None`.

`typing.cast()` is not a substitute for proof. It returns the same object without checking it, so a mistaken cast can hide a bug until runtime.

If a union needs many repeated type checks, I look for a shared protocol or a clearer tagged model. Narrowing should make the legitimate alternatives explicit rather than compensate for an accidental collection of unrelated types.

sections.title: Branches remove possibilities from the type set
sections.content:
A checker tracks a set of possible types at each point in control flow. A successful `isinstance(value, int)` intersects that set with `int`; the false branch removes `int`. A `None` comparison works the same way for optional values. Returns and raises matter because a terminated branch cannot reach later statements.

This is why guard clauses are effective: after `if user is None: return`, every later line in that function sees `user` as a real `User`. The code mirrors the proof a human reader needs and avoids deep nesting.

Narrow with conditions that cannot confuse valid values. `if not count` combines `None`, zero, and other false-like values, so it is unsuitable when zero has meaning. `if count is None` tests exactly the optional state. When the checker cannot infer a complex invariant, a small type guard or a validated domain model may express the proof better than a broad cast.

sections.title: Each branch reduces the remaining types
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[value: int or str or None] --> B{value is None?}
  B -->|Yes| C[Return missing result]
  B -->|No: int or str remains| D{isinstance value, int?}
  D -->|Yes: int| E[Use arithmetic]
  D -->|No: str| F[Use string methods]
```

sections.title: Use guard clauses for clear narrowing
